one_liner: Header-only B-heap priority queue storing priority/payload in separate arrays; faster than std::priority_queue on cache-friendly workloads.
what_it_does: prio_queue is a priority queue replacement built as a B-heap: the underlying array is organized into fixed-size mini-heaps so sift-up/down stays within one or few cache lines instead of striding across the whole array like a binary heap. It keeps the priority key (T) and payload (V) in two parallel arrays rather than one combined struct/pair, and adds a reschedule_top(T) operation (replace-and-resift the top element in one pass) that std::priority_queue lacks. It is not a drop-in: template parameters are ordered differently, push() takes a key or a key+value pair, and top() returns T const& or a pair<T const&, V&> depending on whether a payload type is set.
how_it_is_fast: Core technique is a B-heap layout (mini-heap size tunable as a power of two, e.g. 8/16/32/64) that groups a node's ancestors/descendants into the same cache line, cutting the cache misses a plain array-backed binary heap incurs on deep trees. It pairs this with a 'structure of arrays' split of priority and payload (a custom skip_vector) so comparisons during sift only touch the small, dense priority array and never pull large payload objects into cache. GCC builds additionally use __builtin_expect branch hints on the hot sift loops.
when_to_use: Hot push/pop loops (event queues, schedulers, simulations) with small trivially-copyable priority keys (e.g. int) where std::priority_queue's array-of-struct layout causes cache misses
Workloads where priority and payload can be stored/passed separately via push(key, value) rather than bundled into one pair/struct
Throughput-oriented benchmarking over many push+pop cycles rather than a single latency-critical operation
x86-64 GCC/Clang, C++14+ codebases willing to tune miniheap_size to the target cache line size (64 bytes in the reference hardware)
Projects that want a dependency-free single header they can vendor without pulling in a build system
when_not_to_use: Payload is a large or non-trivial type such as std::pair<int, std::unique_ptr<msg>> — the author's own benchmark shows this configuration can be worse than or comparable to std::priority_queue
You need a stable ordering among equal priorities — it's an unstable B-heap (confirmed by the maintainer in issue #2); add a discriminator field if insertion order matters
You rely on container-adaptor features std::priority_queue doesn't even need to promise here but users may expect: iterators, merge, or swap are not implemented
Concurrent/multi-threaded access — thread safety is not documented and there is no internal synchronization
You need active maintenance: no CI/CMake in the repo, no open issues or PRs, last commit 2025-09-18, and the maintainer said in 2022 he'd probably just use std::vector<> if writing it today

integration.dependencies: none for the library itself (only <vector>, <cassert>, <tuple>, <cstddef>); self_test.cpp and perf_benchmark.cpp additionally pull in Catch2, trompeloeil, and the author's own tachymeter benchmarking header, but none of those are needed to use prio_queue.hpp
integration.min_toolchain: C++14 (uses std::enable_if_t); originally built and benchmarked with g++ 4.9.3 -O3 -std=c++14
integration.platforms: any (portable C++, no SIMD/intrinsics); __builtin_expect is used under __GNUC__ with a no-op fallback elsewhere; miniheap_size should be tuned to the target's cache line size (64 bytes assumed in the reference benchmarks)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; no internal locking, treat as unsynchronized like std::priority_queue
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — different template parameter order, split key/value push and top() API, adds reschedule_top(); call sites need to change, it is not a header swap

gotchas: Not a stable sort: equal-priority elements are not ordered by insertion (maintainer confirmed in issue #2); add an insertion-sequence discriminator to Prio if you need stability
miniheap_size must be a power of two and matched to the CPU cache line / Prio size for the claimed gains; size 8 was 'consistently bad' in the author's own tests
The speedup depends on splitting priority and payload into separate push(key, value) calls; storing both in one struct/pair defeats the optimization and can be slower than std::priority_queue
Exception guarantee is conditional: strong guarantee only if Prio and Value have noexcept move constructors/assignment; otherwise only the weak guarantee (per README)
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick prio_queue when priorities are not monotonically non-decreasing (not a Dijkstra-style access pattern), you need an arbitrary Compare rather than radix bucketing, and you want a tiny dependency-free C++ header. Prefer radix-heap/RadixHeap or S3Q when your workload fits their monotonic-priority or graph-search assumptions — they report larger, more concretely quantified speedups (radix-heap 1.2-1.7x, S3Q 4.6-7x) than this entry's graph-only, unstated ratios.
verified_claims_summary: On an Intel Core i7-4500U (Ubuntu 15.04, 32KB L1d, 64B cache lines) with g++ 4.9.3 -O3 -std=c++14 against libstdc++'s std::priority_queue, the author's blog graphs (no numeric text given) show the B-heap 'always faster' than std::priority_queue<int> across all tested mini-heap sizes (8/16/32/64), and 'consistently much faster' than std::priority_queue<pair<int,int>> when priority/payload are split into separate arrays, over 320 push+pop cycles at increasing queue sizes; the same post reports worse-or-comparable results for a std::pair<int, unique_ptr<msg>> payload.
status_note: Stale: last commit 2025-09-18, no open issues or PRs, and no CI/CMake in the repo, but it's a single BSL-1.0 header small enough to vendor and re-benchmark yourself; the maintainer noted in a 2022 issue he'd likely design it differently (plain std::vector<>) today.
